prompt.context: A large engineering, procurement, and construction company has seen its valuation drop recently. It builds large refineries and industrial plants. It is global in nature and operates in four main regions. This company is a recent roll-up of three smaller companies that operate independently. They have $1B in revenue.
prompt.question: How would you approach the problem of the declining valuation?

clarifying_info.a: Yes, revenue growth is strong both organically and from acquisitions.

clarifying_info.q: What has been happening to margins?

clarifying_info.a: Yes, there is a backlog of work — lots of business.

framework: Revenue Trends: analyze by business unit & region, by product mix, and ability to achieve cross-sell opportunities
Cost Trends: analyze by business unit & region, by product mix, fixed cost synergies, and variable cost synergies
Engineering & Construction Market: assess whether market is growing or shrinking, compare to revenue & cost benchmarks, and review regulatory trends

questions.prompt: What do you think the main potential causes for shrinking margins could be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should approach this with structured analysis, bucketing potential reasons (e.g., revenue, cost, market). Potential causes include: lack of integration of the three units; poor reporting; competing business units; multiple procurement units; lack of cross-selling across units; lack of knowledge sharing across units; high-revenue but unprofitable clients; no prioritization of backlog; sales force compensation structure; declining long-term business need for their services. Excellence is demonstrated by using a structured framework to organize brainstorming rather than listing answers randomly.

questions.prompt: The company thinks they can improve costs after integrating. The goal is to increase margins by 10%. The industry benchmark for optimal utilization is 80% and engineers make $100k each. The three business units have the following engineer counts and utilization rates — BU1: 1,800 engineers at 50% utilization; BU2: 3,000 engineers at 90% utilization; BU3: 1,200 engineers at 50% utilization. Assuming constant man-hours, how many engineers will be needed post-integration?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate effective man-hours per unit, sum them, then divide by the benchmark utilization rate to find the post-integration engineer headcount. This tests the ability to apply a benchmark to a workforce optimization problem.

math.setup: Effective man-hours per BU = # engineers × utilization. Total effective man-hours remains constant post-integration. Post-integration headcount = total effective man-hours ÷ benchmark utilization (80%).
math.answer: 5,250 engineers needed post-integration (vs. 6,000 today), implying a reduction of 750 engineers.

questions.prompt: What would you think are some possible concerns with integrating the three units?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify integration risks such as: different corporate cultures across the three units; different global areas of operations; possibility that units operate in fundamentally different businesses; lack of a sufficient reporting system; whether integration dynamics will be clearly communicated to employees; time frame of integration (e.g., 3 months vs. 3 years). Exceptional candidates will also mention future areas of synergy, e.g., CapEx, administrative costs, PP&E.

brainstorming.prompt: What do you think the main potential causes for shrinking margins could be?

categories.name: Revenue-side issues
ideas: Lack of cross-selling opportunities across the three units
High-revenue but unprofitable clients in the portfolio
No prioritization of backlog leading to lower-margin work being accepted
Sales force compensation structure not aligned with profitability

categories.name: Cost-side issues
ideas: Lack of integration resulting in duplicate procurement units
Multiple overlapping back-office and administrative functions
Lack of knowledge sharing leading to inefficiencies
Poor utilization of engineering workforce across units

categories.name: Structural / management issues
ideas: Poor reporting and visibility into true unit-level profitability
Competing business units undercutting each other on pricing
No consolidated leadership driving synergy realization

categories.name: Market / external issues
ideas: Declining long-term business need for their services

recommendation: The valuation decline is primarily driven by shrinking margins despite strong revenue growth, resulting from the three acquired units operating independently without integration synergies.
Integrating the three business units — starting with procurement consolidation and workforce optimization — can recover margin and restore investor confidence.
risks: Cultural clashes between the three legacy companies could slow integration and reduce employee retention.
The time frame of integration is critical; a poorly managed transition could further disrupt operations and client relationships.
BU2's high utilization (90%) suggests it may be over-stretched; any workforce reduction must be handled carefully to avoid capacity shortfalls.
Units may operate in sufficiently different geographies or sub-markets that full integration is not feasible without business disruption.
next_steps: Conduct a detailed diagnostic of cost and margin by business unit and region to identify the highest-impact synergy opportunities.
Develop an integration roadmap with a realistic timeline (e.g., 18–24 months) covering procurement, reporting systems, and workforce rationalization.
Implement a unified reporting system to provide management visibility into utilization, margins, and client profitability across all units.
Evaluate backlog prioritization criteria to ensure the company is accepting and staffing the most profitable contracts first.
Explore cross-sell opportunities across units to improve revenue quality and client stickiness.
